introduction.1: Many very distinguished minds claim that Cantonese is not a language but a patois. We do not presume to prove that Cantonese is a language; but we think, nevertheless, that it can be considered as one: it is spoken and understood in the provinces of Quang-Tong and Quang-si, and even in Yunnan, under roughly the same conditions as Annamite is spoken in Tonkin, Annam and Cochinchina. There are differences of intonation and pronunciation, and idioms peculiar to each region; but it is none the less true that, knowing the Cantonese spoken on the frontier of Quang-Tong, one is able to understand the Chinese who live around Tonkin and to be understood by them.
introduction.2: We have therefore thought it useful to all those interested in the study of languages to do this work; we hope thereby to spare them the painful and discouraging beginnings that one always encounters here, more than anywhere else, with monosyllabic and tonal languages.
introduction.3: As one advances in the study of Cantonese, one will quite often observe, as we have said, differences of intonation and pronunciation, even with the people of the country where one lives. One may be surprised by this at first, and yet nothing is more natural.
introduction.4: Indeed, when one has lived some time in Tonkin, one is not unaware that races are sometimes very numerous within a small space, and this is particularly the case in the Moncay region. Each race has a language or a patois, but all of them, if they understand Cantonese, do not all speak it in quite the same way.
introduction.5: Thus, in the basin of the Song-Ga-Long and in the small coastal basins extending between the sea and the middle and upper valley of this river, we know of about ten races.
introduction.6: Some undoubtedly have common origins, but living, or above all having lived, separated from one another in the mountains, they have come to no longer know their original language, or to speak it incorrectly, as is the case with the Cantonese language itself.
introduction.7: This is the case of the Xắn giền nhần of the Hacoi sector, considered as brothers by the Annamites, and designated by them under the name Man in the region.
introduction.8: It must also be added that crossings are not rare between these races that have been juxtaposed or superimposed for many years.
introduction.9: One therefore finds in the zone indicated above the:
introduction.10: 1° Hặc nhần. — Apparently the dominant race in China in the two Quang, and perhaps in Yunnan, numerous in the congregation of Maté.
introduction.11: 2° Hặc cá nhần. — Especially at Hacoi.
introduction.12: 3° Ngái nhần. — Especially on the left bank of the Ca-Long, at Na-Luong in China.
introduction.13: 4° Lầu Mần nhần. — At Cai-Lai, Lap-Ma; come, it seems, from Cam-chau in China.
introduction.14: 5° Xắn giền nhần. — At Dai Dien, Lang-Khé; of Annamite origin, commonly called Man by the Annamites of the Delta.
introduction.15: 6° Xắn chỉ nhần. — At Poto, in the Grande-Mamelle, Lang-Tu; probably of Annamite origin, called Thanh-Y by the Annamites and Sagnis or Méo Sagnis by us.
introduction.16: 7° Phền nhần. — At Chu-Phai-San, Hoan Mo; probably of Annamite origin.
introduction.17: 8° Xín nhần. — In the region of Pac-Si.
introduction.18: 9° Thổ nhân. — In the region of Bắc Lạn (north of Bắc Sỉ [?]).
introduction.19: 10° Người An Nam. — The Annamites, along the whole coast.
introduction.20: After this enumeration, perhaps somewhat long, it is easy to realize that it is impossible not to find numerous differences in the spoken language; yet one meets no real difficulty in understanding and in making oneself understood, and that is the essential thing.
introduction.21: We believe we must insist, for, once again, the beginnings are rather painful in the study of the languages of these countries, and, not being forewarned of the few differences one is likely to encounter, one would become discouraged rather quickly and would be wrong to do so, for, in the end, we believe Cantonese easier, that is to say less difficult to learn than Annamite, the intonation not being so rigorous, for a certain number of words, as in the latter language.
introduction.22: The Cantonese language (bặc và, language of the bặc), in our opinion, comes from quan-hoa: the Mandarin language.
introduction.23: Of this latter language we know only the vocabulary made by Lieutenant H. de Lacoste, whose notation is close to that of quốc ngữ. This officer wrote his collection in the district of Lao-Kay.
introduction.24: Each word pronounced by a Miao, a Yao, or a Nhang was noted as it was heard, according to a conventional spelling. Under these conditions one may admit that this quan-hoa, accurate for the upper region, is no more than a corruption of the quan-hoa known in China, and one may even believe it boldly, for Lieutenant de Lacoste noted only three tones, saying moreover that, as Commander Diguet likewise remarked with regard to Tai, the Miao, Yao and Nhang have an ear far more indulgent than the Annamites for faults of intonation, and, we may add, doubtless also than the Chinese of the Quang-Tong frontier, whose hearing is rather delicate, but nevertheless less so than that of the Annamites, certainly because of the variety of races in the country.
introduction.25: Without wishing to make a comparative study of the quan-hoa of the district of Lao-Kay and Cantonese, we think it may be interesting to bring a few words together in order to grasp the differences well and to show the unity of origin; thus we shall take at random:
introduction.27: Innumerable are the words having roughly the same form, and the resemblance would be more perfect if Lieutenant de Lacoste had, like us, adopted the orthography of quốc-ngữ.
introduction.28: This orthography, invented by the Portuguese Fathers to write Annamite, is, in our opinion, the only one that almost perfectly renders the tones and sounds of monosyllabic languages; and had we not wished to borrow it, we would have missed the aim we set ourselves in this study; nevertheless we reserve the right to make a few modifications to it with the sole purpose of simplifying it. We shall give the necessary explanations in due course.
introduction.29: To make the understanding of Cantonese easier, to make its nuances more graspable, we thought it would be very advantageous to have Annamite before one's eyes beside the Chinese. The one will greatly help in better learning the other for the majority of persons living on the frontier; for generally all those whom their occupations force to live in this zone have a more or less extensive smattering of the Annamite language and often have Annamites near them who know quốc-ngữ; moreover, it seems to us that many Annamite words convey the meaning better than periphrases in French.
introduction.30: It will emerge at the same time from this comparison that many Annamite words are of Chinese origin. What form is it fitting to adopt to make this very imperfect study intelligible and practical, above all practical? Shall we group together all words of the same intonation, or place them at random as the pen runs? Neither of these ways seems to us to answer the practical and utilitarian aim we have in view. We think that, in order to facilitate the knowledge of words, it is fitting to group them into what are, as it were, synoptic tables. Thus, in a general way, we shall have brought together all the usual names of animals, of trades or professions, etc. Each table will be followed by conversation exercises. As the case arises, it will always be easy to find quickly the words one needs. But first it is indispensable to study both intonation and pronunciation.
introduction.31: Without entering into too many details on their subject, it is nevertheless necessary to insist somewhat on the one and the other, for to know many words and to ignore intonation and pronunciation is to know nothing. Is it not the same, moreover, for all languages? We shall therefore explain what intonation is; we shall also devote a chapter to pronunciation, being as brief as possible so as not to weary the attention needlessly. We leave it to each person to improve his diction through practice and thus to complete, better than we ourselves could do, the indispensable general indications that we believe we ought to give.
introduction.32: Like the Annamite language, the Chinese language has few grammatical rules. We shall explain them as and when they arise. Is this not the most practical way of learning and retaining them? In every country the child first learns words, and the rules of grammar are learned above all through usage, as and when the child grows older.
introduction.33: That is the right way, we believe; it suffices to complete it by study, that is to say by daily practical exercises. However, to facilitate the work, we shall recapitulate, at the end of the exercises, in succinct tables, the various rules of grammar relating to the article, the substantive, the adjective, the verb, the adverb, etc., which it is important to know. Finally, the word-for-word translation of a few letters and requests will, we believe, happily complete this work.
introduction.34: We think that, presented thus, our study will answer the aim in view: to be essentially practical and utilitarian.

phoneme_description.1: The middle tone, which one pronounces in the ordinary tone of the voice, is not represented by any sign.
phoneme_description.2: The upper tone, higher than the middle tone, is represented by the acute accent.
phoneme_description.3: The lower tone, lower than the middle tone, is represented by a grave accent.
phoneme_description.4: The three compound tones are so named because they partake of the first three.
phoneme_description.5: The upper rising or falling tone. It is pronounced by starting from the middle tone, rising abruptly to the upper tone, and falling, as when one flings out the word 'tiens' to express surprise, for example. This tone is very little used; it is represented by the question-mark sign laid on its side.
phoneme_description.6: The lower rising tone or heavy tone. It is pronounced starting from the lower tone and rising abruptly to the middle tone while noticeably contracting the throat, somewhat in the manner of the English 'ah! aoh!' in comic style. It is represented by a dot under the vowel.
phoneme_description.7: The extended or interrogative rising tone. It is pronounced starting from the lower tone and rising abruptly to the upper tone, with clearly marked interrogation in the voice joined to the surprise of unexpected news, as for example 'ah!' in reply to: so-and-so is dead. This tone is indicated by the question mark.
phoneme_description.8: The quốc ngữ method has allowed us to note the tones; it will now allow us to note the pronunciation, though in a less perfect manner, for some consonants, particularly p and b, are sometimes taken indifferently one for the other by many natives.
phoneme_description.10: Thanks to the beard attached to u and o, one may say that Cantonese possesses eight vowels: a, e, i, o, u, y, ơ, ư.
phoneme_description.11: Their sound varies according to the pronunciation accent with which each may be affected.
phoneme_description.12: The unaccented a is pronounced with the mouth wide open, as in the French words: las, gras.
phoneme_description.13: The â — with circumflex accent — is pronounced short and holds the middle between the French a and e, or more exactly perhaps its sound approaches that of the French words: huin! ham!
phoneme_description.14: with the breve accent — is pronounced with the mouth wide open and briefly, as in French the words: bac, lac.
phoneme_description.15: is pronounced long, as in the French word: baille.
phoneme_description.16: is pronounced short, as in the French word: bail.
phoneme_description.17: is also pronounced short, as in the French words: veille, vaille.
phoneme_description.18: is pronounced long, as in the French word: chaos.
phoneme_description.19: with the circumflex accent on the a — has the same sound, but is pronounced more briefly.
phoneme_description.20: Finally ău holds the middle between au and âu. This diphthong is encountered rather rarely.
phoneme_description.21: The diphthong ao is pronounced by uttering the two letters in succession.
phoneme_description.22: The e without pronunciation accent is pronounced with the mouth open, as in the French words: père, cher. It is the open e. This letter is moreover little used.
phoneme_description.23:
with circumflex accent — is much more common. It is pronounced with the mouth less open, as in the French words: scène, rêne.
It is the closed e.
phoneme_description.24: The diphthongs ei, eo, ea are never encountered. When e follows i = ie, one scarcely hears it pronounced; it is not the same in the diphthong ieu, itself infrequent.
phoneme_description.26: The letter i is commonly encountered; it is subject only to the laws of intonation, so it is useless to insist on its account.
phoneme_description.27: The letter o, very frequent, without pronunciation accent is an open o pronounced by opening the mouth as in the French word hotte.
phoneme_description.28: The ô — with a circumflex accent — is a closed o pronounced as in the French words: clos, rôle.
phoneme_description.29: The bearded ơ. — It is difficult to give its sound exactly, for it is not uniform: in some words it approaches ô, in others, and this is the most general case, it approaches œu in œuf.
phoneme_description.32: The diphthongs oa, oi, ôi, ơi and oai are pronounced by uttering all the letters in succession and as if the i had a diaeresis.
phoneme_description.33: It happens fairly frequently that o and ô are heard for u.
phoneme_description.34: The u is pronounced like ou in French.
phoneme_description.35: The bearded ư is pronounced almost like the French u, advancing the lower lip a little; in certain words the sound approaches that of the French word heu!
phoneme_description.36: It is very rare to find ư at the end of a word as in Annamese, where on the contrary it is frequently encountered.
phoneme_description.37: The diphthongs iu, ieu, ua, ui, ươ, uô are about the only ones used with the letters u and ư. The Annamese language presents more of them: ưa, ue, uê, uoi, ươi, and ươu, which is found only very rarely in Cantonese.
phoneme_description.38: These diphthongs are pronounced by uttering all the letters in succession according to the rules already stated.
phoneme_description.39: The y occurs sometimes, but almost always at the end of words; it is moreover subject to the same laws as i; they sometimes replace one another.
phoneme_description.40:
Taken in isolation, the consonants have the same value as in French, except however the non-barred d, which it is better not to use, r and s. f is replaced by ph and z does not exist. Finally, to render the sounds, two and sometimes three consonants are joined together.
We shall now see the value of these combinations.
phoneme_description.41:
ch — has no equivalent in French; before a vowel it holds the middle between tchi and ti.
At the end of a word, ch indicates a barely perceptible guttural pronunciation.
Moreover it is very seldom encountered in this position, whereas it is very common at the beginning of words.
phoneme_description.42:
The non-barred d has no equivalent in French; moreover it is little used by the Chinese and the words to which it applies belong above all to the quan-hoa language.
It is pronounced like a palatalized gi, trying to make the z heard. Thus it is most often replaced by gi pronounced as just stated.
We even consider it absolutely useless to keep this letter for Cantonese and we shall always replace it with gi.
phoneme_description.43: The barred đ is not necessary for Cantonese: all Annamese words coming from that language and beginning with a đ begin with t in Cantonese.
phoneme_description.44: The gi absolutely takes the place of d and of r in our method. It is pronounced as indicated above.
phoneme_description.45: In some regions gi is replaced by nh or gu, whose value we shall see further on.
phoneme_description.46: The kh is uncommon. It is pronounced by strongly aspirating the h.
phoneme_description.48: Has no equivalent in French; it is found either at the beginning or at the end of the word.
phoneme_description.49: In the first case it is pronounced as if one wrote ngn, softening, or rather crushing, the two n's. If in French one pronounced ngnome (gnome) without the tongue touching the teeth, one would have approximately the pronunciation of ng.
phoneme_description.50: In the second case, at the end of words, it serves as a supporting consonant, thanks to the final g. Without this latter letter the n is pronounced as if it were followed by a mute e in French.
phoneme_description.51: It is to be noted that óng in the word bóng is pronounced almost like áng, báng; it is always thus for similar endings.
phoneme_description.52: The ngh found in Annamese does not exist in Cantonese.
phoneme_description.53: The nh, like the ng, is placed at the beginning or at the end of words.
phoneme_description.54: In the first case, it is pronounced almost like the palatalized French gn.
phoneme_description.55: In the second case, it gives the word the ending gne, as in the word Gascogne.
phoneme_description.56: It sometimes happens that the nh and the ng replace one another, but rarely.
phoneme_description.57: The p, as we said above, is often confused with the b. One may say that these two letters generally form only one which is neither p nor b. Thus one most often writes one for the other.
phoneme_description.58: But it is even more curious to note that sometimes p or b or even t are replaced by x.
phoneme_description.60: These are evidently corruptions of the language, for the standard sentence must be: hi pín xi.
phoneme_description.61: Finally the p sometimes replaces the ph. It is pronounced in a way difficult to describe, approaching p and f by pressing the lips together and opening them abruptly with force.
phoneme_description.62: The letter q is most often replaced by the c.
phoneme_description.63: The letter r is not used; in the few words where one thinks one hears it, it seems more correct to use the g pronounced as a guttural j or palatalized gi.
phoneme_description.64: gềnh, which some Tonkinese would perhaps write renh.
phoneme_description.65: The s is pronounced somewhat like sh or ch in French, but contracting the throat slightly.
phoneme_description.66: This letter is moreover encountered rather rarely; it is advantageously replaced by the letter x.
phoneme_description.67: The t replaces the đ, as we have already seen; or, more exactly, the đ does not exist; t is also sometimes replaced by x.
phoneme_description.68: The th is less common in Chinese than in Annamese; it is often replaced by x. It is pronounced by strongly aspirating the h.
phoneme_description.69: The tr is advantageously replaced by the ch. Perhaps a fine Annamese ear would prefer to hear tran (vrai) instead of chan; but we think it is better to suppress the tr, whose use is moreover infrequent.
phoneme_description.70: The v is a letter one encounters rather seldom. It is pronounced as in French.
phoneme_description.71: The letter x, as we have already seen, is very much used. It replaces above all the s and sometimes the p, the b, the th, etc.
phoneme_description.72: The x is pronounced somewhat in the manner of the English th, placing the front part of the tongue against the teeth.
phoneme_description.73: REMARK. — In all the preceding explanations one should see only general rules, very general rules. As we have already said, the differences in pronunciation are numerous even for a single region. One should therefore not be surprised at the exceptions, doubtless frequent, that one may observe.
phoneme_description.74: It is by practice alone that one learns a language; the book should have no other aim than to facilitate study. Doing thèmes and versions (composition and translation exercises) is still a good means; but we think that
phoneme_description.75: nothing is worth practical exercises, conversation all day long while carefully noting the new words that strike the ear.
phoneme_description.76: By practising speaking without fearing the mocking smiles of the natives, while taking notes at the same time, one will arrive fairly quickly at making very noticeable progress. Grammatical rules are insignificant; it is therefore enough to learn words, many words.
phoneme_description.77: And it will then be easy for one who already knows Annamese to realize very quickly the consonant changes from Cantonese to Annamese: Cantonese t often becomes Annamese d; th, b, p become x, ch, etc.

introduction.1: 好多見識好高嘅人都話，「粵語」唔係一種語言，只係一種方言。我哋冇本事證明「粵語」係一種語言；不過我哋認為，始終可以當佢係一種語言：喺廣東同廣西兩省，甚至喺雲南，都有人講佢、聽得明佢，情況同安南語喺北圻、安南同交趾支那通行嘅差唔多。各地嘅語調同發音都有差異，每個地區都有自己嘅慣用語；但係唔可以否認嘅係，識得廣東邊境通行嘅粵語，就能夠聽明住喺北圻周圍嘅中國人，亦都能夠畀佢哋聽得明。
introduction.2: 所以我哋就諗，做呢份工夫對所有對語言研究有興趣嘅人都有用；我哋希望咁樣可以幫佢哋避開學單音節、有聲調嘅語言時，喺呢度比喺其他任何地方都更加會撞到嘅嗰啲辛苦又令人洩氣嘅開頭。
introduction.3: 我哋講過，隨住粵語學習越嚟越深入，就會幾經常察覺到語調同發音上嘅差異，即使係同自己住喺嗰度嘅本地人都有。開頭或者會覺得詫異，但其實冇乜嘢比呢樣更自然。
introduction.4: 事實係，喺北圻住過一排，就唔會唔知：有時一個細細嘅地方就住咗好多唔同族群，芒街（Moncay）一帶尤其係咁。每個族群都有自己嘅語言或者方言，但佢哋就算聽得明粵語，講起上嚟都唔係完全一樣。
introduction.5: 譬如，喺嘉隆江（Song-Ga-Long）流域，同埋喺海同呢條河嘅中游、上游河谷之間伸延嘅啲細細嘅沿海盆地，我哋知道有成十個左右嘅族群。
introduction.6: 當中有啲無疑係同源嘅，但係佢哋喺山入面生活，或者長久以嚟主要都係各自分開住，結果就搞到唔再識自己原本嘅語言，或者講得唔多正確，就好似粵語本身咁。
introduction.7: 河檜（Hacoi）一帶嘅 Xắn giền nhần 就係咁：安南人當佢哋係兄弟，仲喺嗰區叫佢哋做 Man（蠻）。
introduction.8: 仲要加多句，呢啲毗鄰而居、或者多年以嚟疊住一齊住嘅族群之間，通婚混血並唔罕見。
introduction.9: 所以喺上面講到嘅範圍之內，可以搵到以下呢幾種：
introduction.10: 1° Hặc nhần。—— 睇嚟係兩廣、可能連雲南都算在內嘅中國主導族群，喺 Maté 教區人數好多。
introduction.11: 2° Hặc cá nhần。—— 主要喺河檜（Hacoi）。
introduction.12: 3° Ngái nhần。—— 主要喺嘉隆江（Ca-Long）左岸，中國境內嘅那良（Na-Luong）。
introduction.13: 4° Lầu Mần nhần。—— 喺 Cai-Lai、Lap-Ma；聽講係由中國欽州（Cam-chau）嚟嘅。
introduction.14: 5° Xắn giền nhần。—— 喺 Dai Dien、Lang-Khé；原籍安南，三角洲嘅安南人通常叫佢哋做 Man（蠻）。
introduction.15: 6° Xắn chỉ nhần。—— 喺 Poto，即 Grande-Mamelle（大乳房山）一帶、Lang-Tu；大概原籍安南，安南人叫佢哋 Thanh-Y，我哋就叫佢哋 Sagnis 或者 Méo Sagnis。
introduction.16: 7° Phền nhần。—— 喺 Chu-Phai-San、Hoan Mo；大概原籍安南。
introduction.17: 8° Xín nhần。—— 喺 Pac-Si 地區。
introduction.18: 第九：首人（Thủ nhần）。喺 Bac-Lan 地區（Pac-Si 以北）。
introduction.19: 第十：安南人（Ốn nàm nhần）。成條海岸線都有。
introduction.20: 喺呢個可能長咗少少嘅列舉之後，好容易就睇得出：喺口語入面，冇可能搵唔到好多差異；但係要聽得明人哋講乜、又要人哋聽得明自己講乜，並唔會遇到真正嘅困難，而呢點先至係最緊要嘅。
introduction.21: 我哋覺得一定要強調一下，因為，再講一次，學呢啲國家嘅語言，開頭係幾辛苦嘅；如果事先唔知道可能會遇到嘅嗰啲差異，人就好快會洩氣，噉就錯喇；因為講到底，我哋認為粵語比較容易，即係比安南語冇咁難學，對唔少字嚟講，佢嘅聲調冇安南語咁嚴。
introduction.22: 我哋認為，粵語（bặc và，即 bặc 人嘅語言）係源自官話（quan-hoa），即官話。
introduction.23: 講到官話呢種語言，我哋淨係識 H. de Lacoste 中尉編嘅詞彙表，佢嘅標音同國語字（quốc ngữ）嘅標音幾接近。呢位軍官係喺老街（Lao-Kay）轄區寫成佢嗰本集嘅。
introduction.24: 苗人（Méo）、瑤人（Yao）或者 Nhang 人每講一個字，都係照聽到嘅樣，用一套約定俗成嘅拼寫記落嚟。喺噉嘅情況下，可以話呢種喺高地區域準確嘅官話，只不過係中國通行嘅官話嘅一個訛變版本；甚至可以大膽噉相信，因為 de Lacoste 中尉淨係記低咗三個聲調。佢仲話——正如 Diguet 少校講到泰語（taï）嗰陣亦都同樣留意到——苗人、瑤人同 Nhang 人對聲調錯誤嘅耳朵，比安南人寬容得多；我哋大概仲可以加多句：廣東（Quang-Tong）邊境嘅中國人聽覺都幾敏銳，但始終冇安南人咁利，肯定係因為嗰度種族混雜嘅緣故。
introduction.25: 我哋唔係想對老街轄區嘅官話同粵語做比較研究，但係覺得攞幾個字嚟對照一下會幾有意思，可以好好噉捉到啲差異，同埋顯示出佢哋同出一源；噉我哋就隨便攞：
introduction.27: 字形差唔多一樣嘅字多到數唔晒；如果 de Lacoste 中尉好似我哋噉採用國語字（quốc-ngữ）嘅拼寫，啲字就會似得更加完美。
introduction.28: 呢套拼寫法係葡萄牙神父為咗寫安南語而發明嘅；我哋認為，佢係唯一可以幾乎完美噉表達單音節語言嘅聲調同語音嘅拼寫法。即使我哋唔想借用佢，都會達唔到我哋喺呢項研究入面定下嘅目標。不過，我哋會保留對佢做少少改動嘅權利，目的淨係為咗簡化佢。到適當嘅時候，我哋會作出必要嘅解釋。
introduction.29: 為咗令人更易明白粵語，為咗令人更易捉到佢嘅細微分別，我哋覺得將安南語擺喺中文隔籬一齊睇，會好有好處。對於住喺邊境嘅大多數人嚟講，一種語言會大大幫助佢哋學好另一種；因為一般而言，所有因為生計被迫喺呢個地帶居住嘅人，都或多或少帶啲安南語嘅底子，而且身邊經常有識國語字（quốc-ngữ）嘅安南人；另外，我哋覺得好多安南語詞，比起用法文兜圈講，更加能夠表達箇中意思。
introduction.30: 從呢個對照亦可以睇出，好多安南語詞都係源自中文。究竟要採用邊種形式，先可以令呢份極唔完善嘅研究易明又實用，尤其係實用呢？我哋要將所有同聲調嘅字歸埋一堆，抑或隨手寫到邊擺到邊？我哋覺得呢啲做法都達唔到我哋心目中所追求嘅實用同功利目標。我哋認為，為咗方便認識啲字詞，應該將佢哋編成一啲可以話係一覽表嘅表格。噉樣，一般嚟講，我哋就會將動物、行業或者職業等等嘅常用名詞集合埋一齊。每個表之後都會跟住有會話練習。視乎情況，要快手搵到需要用嘅字詞，永遠都咁容易。不過喺呢之前，一定要研究聲調同發音。
introduction.31: 雖然唔想就呢兩樣講得太詳細，但係仍然有必要對聲調同發音稍為強調一下，因為識好多字但唔理聲調同發音，等於乜都唔識。再講，所有語言唔都係一樣咩？所以我哋會解釋乜嘢係聲調；亦會撥一章嚟講發音，盡量簡短，免得無謂咁搞到人哋攰。至於透過練習改善自己嘅咬字，藉此補充我哋認為必須指出嘅嗰啲不可或缺嘅一般說明——呢啲就留返畀各人自己去做，做得比我哋自己仲好。
introduction.32: 同安南語一樣，中文都冇乜語法規則。我哋會喺佢哋出現嘅時候逐一解釋。噉唔係學同記佢哋最實用嘅方法咩？喺所有國家，細路都係先學字詞，而語法規則主要係隨住細路大個、透過使用嚟學嘅。
introduction.33: 我哋相信，噉先至係好方法；只要透過學習，即係每日嘅實際練習，去補足就得。不過，為咗方便做嘢，我哋會喺練習最後，用簡明嘅表格總結各種必須認識嘅語法規則，包括冠詞、名詞、形容詞、動詞、副詞等等。最後，我哋相信，將幾封信同幾份呈文逐字逐句翻譯出嚟，會圓滿噉完成呢份工作。
introduction.34: 我哋相信，噉樣呈現嘅呢份研究，會達到預期嘅目標：基本上做到實用同功利。
